new_statements.quote: In a verb, the stressed syllable is usually the verb itself, as opposed to any prefix or suffix. If, however, a suffix ending with {'} is separated from the verb by at least one other suffix, both the verb and the suffix ending in {'} are stressed. In addition, if the meaning of any particular suffix is to be emphasized, the stress may shift to that syllable. [...] In a noun, the stressed syllable is usually the syllable right before the first noun suffix, or the final syllable if there is no suffix. If, however, a syllable ending in {'} is present, it is usually stressed instead. If there are two syllables in a row {'} both ending in {',} both are equally stressed.
new_statements.citation: Okrand, Marc. 1992. The Klingon Dictionary: English/Klingon, Klingon/English. 2nd ed. New York: Pocket Books (ISBN 0-671-74559-X), section 1.3 'Stress', pp. 17-18.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Klingonska Akademien proofread scanned transcription of Okrand 1992, The Klingon Dictionary, 2nd ed., Pocket Books, ISBN 0-671-74559-X; header lists the book's identity and the 2000-2020 correction log). Surrounding text read: "Each Klingon word of more than one sylla…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per polysyllabic word, realised by higher pitch and more force. Stress is morphologically anchored: in verbs it falls on the verb root (never on the pronominal prefix or suffixes by default); in nouns it falls on the last syllable of the noun stem (the syllable before the first noun suffix, or the final syllable of an unsuffixed noun). Overriding this, any syllable closed by the glottal stop {'} attracts stress (in verbs, a {'}-final suffix separated from the root by another suffix takes stress alongside the root; in nouns a {'}-final syllable is 'usually stressed instead'; two adjacent {'}-final syllables are both stressed). Pragmatic emphasis can shift stress to a suffix; negation/emphatic rovers and the interrogative suffix are frequently stressed. Stress is not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as 'secondary'; but the source allows two stressed syllables in one word: verb root plus a {'}-final suffix separated from it ('both.. are stressed'), and two adjacent {'}-final syllables 'both are equally stressed'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'there are some words which seem to have variable stress patterns, with the stress sometimes heard on one syllable and sometimes on another. This phenomenon is not yet understood.' Stress may also shift to any suffix whose meaning is emphasised; negation/emphasis suffixes (sect. 4.3) and the interrogative suffix (4.2.9) are frequently stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Each Klingon word of more than one syllable normally contains one stressed (or accented) syllable'); rules given separately for verbs and nouns; no phrase-level statement. Stress is not indicated in the transcription system. Quote is from a fan scanned transcription (Klingonska Akademien, proofread 2000-2020) of the printed book, not a page scan; the stray '{'}' before 'both ending in' in the last sentence is a transcription artefact.
new_statements.identity_note: Klingon is a constructed language (Marc Okrand for Paramount's Star Trek films, 1984-); Glottolog 5.1 classes it under 'Artificial Language' and lists no descriptive references. The description is of Okrand's standard variety (ta' Hol); KGT 1997 mentions regional 'accents' (Krotmag, Morska etc.) but these concern segments, not stress. Whether a conlang belongs in the catalog is a policy decision for the parent; the stress statement itself is first-hand and explicit.

new_statements.quote: In a verb, the stress normally falls on the verb root itself; however, a suffix which ends with ' (the apostrophe) will also get stress. If the meaning of a particular verb suffix is to be emphasized, then the stress may shift to the suffix, even if it does not end with '. [...] In a noun, the final syllable of the root noun is usually stressed. However, if a noun suffix ends with ', that will usually get the stress instead of the root noun's final syllable. If two syllables in a row end with ', they are equally stressed. [...] There is some variability with stress patterns that is not completely understood.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not yet in the catalog (catalog_records empty). The page restates the existing statement from Okrand 1992 TKD section 1.3 pp. 17-18 (root stress in verbs, root-final stress in nouns, {'}-final suffixes stressed, emphasis shift, unexplained variability) with the same placements, and adds audio-tape evidence (verb stressed before -jaj; tlhIngan initial, tera'ngan on the {'} syllable, 'ngan is never stressed'; Ha'DIbaH initial). It is a fan-wiki restatement of TKD, not an independent source; compatible, adds examples only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is assigned morphologically: in verbs it falls on the verb root (not on prefixes or suffixes); in nouns on the final syllable of the noun root. A suffix whose syllable ends in the glottal stop {'} attracts stress as well (and a suffix can be stressed for emphasis); two adjacent {'}-final syllables are equally stressed. The page adds observations from Okrand's audio tapes: the verb before the suffix -jaj is stressed; tlhIngan is stressed on the first syllable, tera'ngan on the {'}-final second syllable, so the syllable ngan is never stressed; Ha'DIbaH is stressed on its {'}-final first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the page says two consecutive {'}-final syllables are 'equally stressed', and a {'}-final suffix is stressed alongside the root (double prominence), but no secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Emphasis can shift stress to a suffix (e.g. -qu' or a negation suffix); 'some variability with stress patterns that is not completely understood', possibly dialectal or from assimilated non-Klingon speakers; Gowron's pronunciation on the Star Trek: Klingon CD is noted as arguably non-canonical.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Okrand's standard (canonical) Klingon as in The Klingon Dictionary and the Conversational Klingon / Power Klingon tapes; the wiki mentions possible dialectal variation but describes no particular dialect. The wiki's Gowron example (Star Trek: Klingon CD) is flagged by the page itself as of disputed canonicity.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Klingon language', section Phonology > Stress (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Okrand 1992 (TKD) p. 17.
sources.note: Paraphrases TKD 1.3: verbs stressed on the verbal stem, plus any {'}-final suffix separated by another suffix; nouns stressed on the final stem syllable, shifting to {'}-final syllables; other words variable but mostly monosyllabic. Second-hand summary of the primary source (this is what the earlier scan read).

sources.citation: Okrand, Marc. 1997. Klingon for the Galactic Traveler. New York: Pocket Books. ISBN 0-671-00995-8.
sources.note: No stress rule restated; incidental only: younger speakers reduce doubled consonants in qettaH / bommey 'with stress remaining on the first syllable' (pp. 138-139), unstressed a may centralise to [U] (p. 139); regional 'accents' (Krotmag etc., p. 26 ff.) concern segments, not stress.
